title: Garter stitch lap throw
subtitle: A 100 by 120 cm DK lap throw in all-garter, single panel.
excerpt: A 100 by 120 cm lap throw worked flat in plain garter stitch on 4 mm needles, using approximately 750 g of DK wool. The same technique as the baby blanket, scaled to lap-throw proportions.
sourceNotes: Weldon's Practical Knitter, 3rd series (1887), §Knitted Blankets and Covers, documents single-panel garter throws in standard worsted or double-knitting weight as a common Victorian home-knitting project. The same proportions appear in later domestic manuals including Elizabeth Zimmermann's Knitting Without Tears (1971), §Afghans.

knitting.gaugeText: 22 sts × 44 rows = 10 × 10 cm in garter stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A knitted blanket sized to cover the lap of one seated person, typically 90 to 130 cm wide by 100 to 150 cm long. Intended for a sofa, armchair, or reading chair rather than a full bed.

content.text: A single-panel
lap throw
worked flat in garter stitch on 4 mm needles in DK wool, finishing at 100 cm wide by 120 cm long.

A single panel requires no seaming; the knitter casts on the full width and works in a single strip to the finished length. Garter stitch was chosen for the same reason it serves the baby blanket: it lies flat without blocking, both faces look identical, and the stitch is entirely knit. At DK weight this is a longer undertaking than the chunky version, but the finer fabric drapes more softly and folds flatter. A DK garter throw is the long-evening project, the companion to an audiobook or a film series. Budget about 750 g (about 1,650 m / 1,800 yards) of DK wool or wool blend. This blanket draws from five or six skeins; buy all of them at once in matched dye lots and alternate skeins every two rows to average any lot drift. Drapes over a sofa end or folds to a manageable rectangle for storage.
What you need

items.name: Yarn
items.qty: 750 g (about 1,650 m / 1,800 yards) of DK-weight wool or wool blend
items.substitutions: 100% wool DK or an 80% wool blend. Superwash is optional for a lap throw used by adults; if it will go in the machine wash, choose superwash. Avoid pure acrylic DK for a project this size: the throw will be heavy and pill quickly.

items.name: Needles
items.qty: 4 mm (UK 8 / US 6) circular needle, 120 cm or longer (the blanket is wide; a long cable is more comfortable than a short one)

content.text: Gauge
22 stitches and 44 rows to 10 cm over garter stitch on 4 mm needles, unblocked. Work a 15 cm square swatch, leave it flat overnight, and measure the centre 10 cm.

If your stitch gauge is 20 per 10 cm with a 220-stitch cast-on, the throw will be about 110 cm wide rather than 100 cm. Adjust the cast-on count for your target width (multiply 100 by your stitch gauge per 10 cm). At 44 row gauge, a throw 120 cm long requires 528 rows; at 40 row gauge it requires 480 rows. Measure by tape rather than by row count.
Stitches used
Pattern
Cast-on

Using the long-tail cast-on, cast on 220 stitches. Long-tail tail: (4 × 220) / 10 + 15 = 88 + 15 = 103 cm. Measure 120 cm of tail; round up to 140 cm to be comfortable. A 220-stitch blanket cast-on is long enough that running out of tail partway through is a real risk; measure generously.
Body
Knit every row until the throw measures 120 cm from the cast-on edge.

This is a long project. When you set this aside between sessions, every row is a knit row so there is nothing to track. A row marker kept on the needle is useful for counting how many rows you have worked in a sitting; otherwise simply measure the length.
Stitch count check-ins
At row 264 (about 60 cm): count across the needle. You should have 220 stitches. A 220-stitch row count is worth verifying at the halfway point before more than half the yarn is used.
At row 525 (about 119 cm): count again before the final cast-off.
Common faults

Tension tightening over a long session: hands tire and grip the needle harder as a session progresses. A DK lap throw knit in one or two long sittings will show visible tension bands where one sitting ended and the next began. Knit in shorter sessions and take a break when tension starts to tighten.

Dye-lot shift mid-blanket: at this scale, five or six skeins are needed and the risk of a shift is significant. Alternate two skeins every two rows from the start, even within the same nominal dye lot.

Centre-pull balls collapsing and tangling: large DK skeins often come as centre-pull balls. As the ball empties, the centre collapses into a tangle. Wind each skein into a firm ball before starting. Use a ball winder if you have one, or pull from the outside of the skein instead.
Cast-off
Cast off all 220 stitches knitwise with a relaxed tension. A cast-off this long benefits from working 50 stitches, pausing to check the tension, and adjusting before continuing.
Finishing

Weave in the cast-on and cast-off tails and any yarn-join tails on the wrong side along garter ridges, running each tail at least 5 cm and changing direction once. Garter stitch lies flat without blocking; a gentle wash and flat dry will even out any tension variation.
Care

Hand wash in cool water for non-superwash wool. Machine wash on a gentle 30-degree cycle for superwash DK. Lay flat to dry; a wet DK throw is too heavy to hang without distorting. Allow several hours to dry fully.
What to try next

The natural next project from a plain DK garter throw is a striped version: the same cast-on and construction but two or three colours alternating every four rows. Because the throw is wide and long, bold stripe colours read well from across the room. After that, a cabled lap throw uses the same DK weight and a similar width but introduces a cable column in the centre, framed by seed-stitch side panels.
